what_its_for: Lamivudine is an antiviral medicine used to treat two different infections. Epivir is used to treat HIV (the virus that causes AIDS) — it helps keep the virus under control so your immune system can stay stronger. Epivir-HBV is used to treat chronic hepatitis B, a long-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus. This medicine does not cure these infections, but it helps keep them under control.
how_to_take: Take lamivudine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food — food does not affect how well it works. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water. If you are taking the liquid form, use the measuring cup or oral syringe that comes with the medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take this medicine at the same time every day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel fine.
dosing: Your dose depends on what condition you are being treated for, your weight, your age, and how well your kidneys are working. Common doses are: For HIV in adults — 150 mg twice a day OR 300 mg once a day. For hepatitis B in adults — 100 mg once a day. Children's doses are based on body weight. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Missing doses can let the virus grow and make the medicine less effective, so try to take it every day as scheduled.
storage: Store lamivudine tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Do not take lamivudine with other medicines that also contain lamivudine, such as Combivir, Epzicom, Triumeq, or Trizivir — this could give you too much of the drug. Do not take Epivir (HIV dose) and Epivir-HBV (hepatitis B dose) at the same time. Avoid drinking alcohol heavily, as it can make liver problems worse. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, because some medicines can interact with lamivudine, especially other HIV or hepatitis medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you notice: unusual muscle pain, weakness, or trouble breathing; stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or feeling very cold; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet (signs of nerve problems); fast or irregular heartbeat; feeling dizzy or lightheaded; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, or severe tiredness; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. If you have hepatitis B and stop taking lamivudine, your hepatitis B may suddenly get worse — contact your doctor immediately if this happens.
when_it_works: Lamivudine starts working right away in your body, but you may not feel a difference at first. For HIV, it helps reduce the amount of virus in your blood (viral load) and can improve your immune system (CD4 count) over several weeks to months. For hepatitis B, it helps reduce liver inflammation and the amount of virus in your blood over weeks to months. It is important to keep taking the medicine every day even when you feel well — stopping early can make the virus come back or become resistant to the medicine.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If your kidneys do not work well, your doctor may lower your dose or change how often you take it. Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease. Liver problems: Use with caution in people with liver disease. If you have hepatitis B and also have HIV, make sure your doctor knows — the correct dose and medicine combination is very important. Pregnancy: Lamivudine is commonly used during pregnancy to help prevent passing HIV to a baby. Talk to your doctor about the benefits and risks. Breastfeeding: Women with HIV should not breastfeed to avoid passing the virus to the baby. Talk to your doctor. Older adults: Older patients may need dose adjustments depending on kidney function. Children: Liquid form is available for children — the dose is based on the child's weight.
